analysis.one_liner: Makes credit freezes and fraud alerts free and lasts years after the Equifax breach.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a vote, even after the committee held a hearing on it.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2017 Equifax hack, this bill would have let anyone freeze their credit file for free, so thieves couldn't open loans in their name. It would have extended the standard fraud alert from 90 days to a full year, made credit bureaus process freezes and unfreezes quickly, given an extra free credit report, and refunded the fees people paid for freezes after the breach. It never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose personal data was exposed in the Equifax breach or any future breach. A credit freeze blocks the credit bureaus from releasing your file to open new credit without your permission, which is one of the strongest tools against identity theft. The bill also helps people who had already paid the bureaus' freeze fees by requiring refunds.

how_it_helps.text: Requires credit bureaus to place a free credit freeze on request, and bans any fee to place, temporarily lift, or fully remove a freeze [S2][S3].
Extends the standard fraud alert from 90 days to one year, renewable on request, and expands the seven-year alert for identity theft victims [S2][S3].
Sets deadlines for the bureaus: a freeze must be placed within one business day, and lifting it by phone or online must happen within 15 minutes [S3].
Gives consumers an extra free credit report whenever they request a freeze [S2][S3].
Requires refunds of any freeze fees charged between September 7, 2017 and enactment, and bars fees for lifting or removing freezes already in place [S2].
Keeps frozen consumers off the marketing lists the bureaus sell to companies pitching credit and insurance offers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The three big credit bureaus — Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — which charged consumers roughly $10 or more per state to place or lift a freeze, and which sell prescreen marketing lists. They would lose that fee revenue and the list sales.

drawbacks.text: The bill only strengthens consumer tools after a breach; it does not require the bureaus to better secure the data in the first place, so breaches can still happen [S2][S3].

A freeze can inconvenience consumers applying for new credit, mortgages, or phone service, since the freeze must be lifted first — the bill limits this with 15-minute electronic lifts and exceptions for existing accounts, insurance, and employment checks, but some friction remains [S3].
The bureaus bear the administrative cost of free, fast freeze processing and refunds, and industry would argue those costs get built into their operations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls on the credit bureaus, not on ordinary people, and the benefit — a free, fast lock on your own credit file — is real protection against identity theft in an era of routine data breaches. The main honest criticism is that it treats symptoms: it doesn't force companies like Equifax to secure data better in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held one hearing on it, but the committee never voted on it and it never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced September 14, 2017 by Sen. Elizabeth Warren with 11 original cosponsors, about a week after Equifax disclosed its breach [S1][S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, where it stayed [S5].
The committee held a hearing on October 17, 2017, but never marked the bill up or reported it out [S5].
It gathered 18 cosponsors (17 Democrats and 1 independent) but no Senate Republican, and no floor vote ever happened before the 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019 [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The credit bureaus, which kept charging freeze fees after the breach. Consumers ultimately got free freezes from a different, broader banking bill in 2018, but this one died without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The credit bureaus, which kept their fees

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Sen. Sanders; no Senate Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired Banking Committee never moved it to a vote [S1][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill bans the fees they charged consumers to freeze and unfreeze their own files, requires refunds of fees paid after the Equifax breach, and sets fast deadlines for processing. It hits them exactly where the breach made consumers pay them more.

industries.industry: Prescreen marketing lists (credit and insurance offer marketers)
industries.note: The bureaus would be barred from including frozen consumers in the lists they sell to companies making unsolicited credit and insurance offers, cutting off that marketing channel for frozen files.
